This paper provides the first empirical test of how characteristics of extreme weather events shape the geographic areas within which people are most likely to report they personally experienced the event.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the perceived experience of extreme weather is shaped by both the characteristics of the extreme weather events and the characteristics of the people who report experiencing them.

we found that people are likely to perceive that they have experienced extreme events if the events are nearby, intense, and last a long time.
The main takeaway from our work is that

there are clear differences in the geographic extent of the "shadow of experience" for different types of extreme weather events, with hurricanes and tornadoes having a much larger shadow of experience than drought.
